Put the framing in one paragraph and the conclusions drawn from it in the next.
The framing is the setup the conclusions rest on:
the definitions, the given [function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/functions.html#def-function) or data,
and the quantities computed from them, such as a gradient.
A conclusion is a statement the framing implies.

A reader who meets a conclusion in the middle of the setup
cannot tell which sentences define the problem and which ones report a result.
A separate paragraph for each lets the reader take in the setup first,
then see what follows from it.

::: {#exm-framing-apart-from-conclusions}

## Separating the setup from the stationary point

> ❌ Let $f(\vx) = x_1^2 - x_2^2$.
> Its gradient is $\gradf{f}(\vx) = \tp{(2 x_1,\ -2 x_2)}$, which is $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ only at $\vx = \vzero_{2 \times 1}$,
> so $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ is a stationary point.
>
> ✅ Let $f(\vx) = x_1^2 - x_2^2$.
> Its gradient is
>
> $$
> \gradf{f}(\vx) = \tp{(2 x_1,\ -2 x_2)}.
> $$
>
> The gradient $\gradf{f}(\vx)$ is $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ only at $\vx = \vzero_{2 \times 1}$,
> so $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ is a stationary point.

In the ❌ version, one sentence defines $f$, computes its gradient, locates its zero, and concludes.
In the ✅ version, the first paragraph holds the framing,
which is $f$ and its gradient,
and the second holds the conclusion.

:::
